Every field service job has three people asking questions at different times.

The office: who's free, and who's closest?
The technician: where am I going next, and what's the job?
The customer: when will they actually get here?

ArrivePing puts one job on three screens. The office assigns it, the tech gets it on their phone, and the moment they tap "on the way," the customer gets a text with a live tracking link.

We wrote up what that tracking link should and shouldn't show customers, including the privacy line we never cross:
https://arriveping.com/blog/what-should-a-customer-tracking-link-show

The service window was never really about service. It exists because the office can't promise what it can't see.

Once the office can see where every tech is, the promise changes from "between 8 and 12" to "about 3 minutes out," sent automatically when the tech heads over.

Customers don't need the whole day blocked off. They need to know when to be at the door.

The checklist for what that message and tracking link should include:

posts.text:
What should your customer see when they tap the tracking link?

Our answer, from building one: a live ETA, the address, the tech's name, a way to call or text them, and a timeline of the job so far.

What they should not see: the tech's location before they're on the way to that job, or after they've arrived. Tracking only works if your techs trust it as much as your customers do.

The full checklist, with sources:
https://arriveping.com/blog/what-should-a-customer-tracking-link-show

Most dispatch tools are built around today. Small teams live in the week.

The job you push from Tuesday has to land somewhere. The install that runs long eats Thursday morning. ArrivePing's week view shows every tech's days side by side, so you can move work before it collides instead of after.

posts.text:
Here's a simple way to check whether $49 a month makes sense for your team.

Say an hour of your time costs about $35 once wages, payroll taxes and overhead are counted. That is an assumption, so swap in your own number. At $35 an hour, $49 a month is 84 minutes. Spread over 21 working days, that's about 4 minutes a day.

Four minutes is one "where's the tech?" call you don't have to take, or one customer who is home when you arrive instead of out.

We wrote up the full math, with every input labelled, plus a five-question test for whether you need field service software at all (and when a spreadsheet is still enough):
https://arriveping.com/blog/does-your-business-need-field-service-software
